Variants.Content: The cities of Slaver's Bay have long been ruled by the Ghiscari master class: the Good Lord of Astapor, the Wise Lord of Yunkai, and the Great Lord of Meereen maintain similar high positions with different titles, live in pyramid mansions, and control land, trade, military training, and the slave market. Below them are free merchants, craftsmen, secretaries, mercenaries and dependents, and below them are slaves with a large number and complex sources. From domestic servants, miners, field slaves to trained soldiers, they are all distinguished by price and use. Abolition of slavery can interrupt buying and selling, but it will not instantly eliminate wealth, skills, resentment, and supply dependence; old owners may hide assets, and freed people must also fight for food, wages, shelter, and political voice. Any new order must face the realities left behind by these layers.

The master class often spoke of hierarchy as the natural order in which the city flourished, emphasizing that the pyramids, irrigation, and trade were maintained by them. When they lose their privileges, the first thing they resort to is often not morality, but food prices, public security and old contracts.

Slaves and freedmen did not understand order to be the same thing. Being able to leave your master is only the first step; without wages, shelter, and the power to protect yourself from retaliation, freedom can easily turn into another form of hunger.

Soldiers look at who can pay, clerks look at who controls the roster, and priests look at who can interpret God's will. Every change in the politics of Slaver's Bay had to go through these intermediaries before actually entering the streets and fields.

Entry Slaver's Bay Society Social Hierarchy of Slaver's Bay: The pyramidal nobility, merchant trade, freedmen and the large slave population were interdependent, and emancipation or restoration would touch the entire urban structure. Whether it is valid depends on who can grant the rights, collect the consideration, and actually make the judgment come to fruition in the event of default.
